/Issued 258 PM MDT Tue Jul 28 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

Strong upper-level ridging will continue through the rest of the
week keeping temperatures hot and funneling more smoke from
wildfires in the PacNW into Montana. Monsoonal moisture lifting 
up and around the ridge will provide daily chances for afternoon 
thunderstorms with the main threat being lightning and strong 
gusts. Otherwise dry conditions will persist for most areas with 
low minimum relative humidity through the afternoon.

The ridge starts to break down this weekend as a strong trough
moves into the region bringing strong winds to the region,
particularly along the Rocky Mountain Front. A brief cool down is
expected for Monday before things slowly start to warm back up
again heading towards the middle of next week as another ridge
tries to build across the western CONUS.  -thor


 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Thunderstorm Chances This Week...

Isolated to scattered thunderstorms are possible Wednesday and
Thursday afternoon across Southwest Montana with some isolated
thunderstorms possible further north. The uncertainty in the
forecast centers around how thick the smoke is over the region. It
is possible the smoke could limit thunderstorm development either
partially or entirely depending on how things play out. But the
main concern is that any thunderstorm that develops will be on the
drier side which will increase fire weather concerns, especially 
if there is frequent cloud to ground lightning. The potential for 
severe weather remains quite low at this time but a stray gust up 
to 70 mph cannot be ruled out as DCAPE is over 1500 J/kg for a 
good portion of the region.

Outside of this potential most areas will remain dry through the
rest of the week.   -thor


Return of Extreme Temperatures by Saturday...

While temperatures will remain hot through the remainder of the work 
week climate anomaly indicators have honed in on Saturday being the 
hottest day of the upcoming week, with values becoming unusual to 
very unusual with respect to late July/early August climatology. The 
fact that these climate anomaly indicators are suggesting another 
period of hot temperatures is remarkable considering that August 1st 
is (at most locations) only one day past the climatological peak for 
average high temperatures across Southwest through North Central 
Montana. The table below represents the potential high temperature 
scenarios for select cities across Southwest through North Central 
Montana, with the "Low End" scenario being the NBM10Pct (10% chance 
that temperatures are lower than the listed value), "Most Likely" 
scenario being the NBM50Pct, and the "High End" scenario being the 
NBM90Pct (10% chance that temperatures exceed the listed value).

                    Saturday's High Temperature Scenarios
LOCATION               Low End | Most Likely | High End
Browning                  88   |      93     |     98
Cut Bank                  95   |     100     |    104
Havre                    103   |     108     |    111
Great Falls              102   |     105     |    107
Lewistown                 98   |     101     |    104
Helena                    97   |     100     |    104
White Sulphur Springs     95   |     102     |    101       
Bozeman                   98   |      98     |    105
Dillon                    95   |      98     |    100
Ennis                     94   |      98     |    100
West Yellowstone          89   |      93     |     96

Given the presence of regional wildfires across the Northern Rockies 
the "High End" scenario will be tough to reach due to decreased 
solar insolation from the smoke, with dense smoke having the ability 
to hold temperatures back some 5 to 10 degrees.


Strong Winds from Saturday night through Sunday...

Confidence is increasing that a period of strong, nearing high, 
winds will impact the Rocky Mountain Front from Saturday night 
through the day on Sunday due to the combination of mountain wave 
activity (from the late evening hours on Saturday through Sunday 
morning) and deep mixing (during the daylight hours on Sunday). 
H700 winds per NAEFS analysis are prog'd to reach 40-50kts from 
Saturday evening through Sunday morning across the aforementioned 
area, which is 2 to nearly 3 standard deviations above normal. The
table below are the NBM5.0 probabilities for wind gusts to exceed
